doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

chapter: Coming up on the L.A. scene
title: Quitting the NBC day job to make a record date
summary: The NBC job came through his mom; he quit when they would not let him off for a professional recording session, and at 19 was getting calls with Red Mitchell and Gary Peacock.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Did you reach a point as a young man that you could make a living, live on your own by playing the drums? When did that occur?

I figured out that it was possible, and that’s what I wanted to do. So I had this day job at NBC, which my mom would help me get, and I was happy working there. And you know if you join NBC at a lesser capacity, like the mail room or the parking lot, you essentially would be in the organization and then they — when they found a place they’d maybe move you up to something more, you know better in the business. And my dad had worked for NBC for years so you know I got hired because the president of NBC told them to hire me, because he was friends with my mom. So I didn’t want to do that. I wanted to do the job but I wanted to hang out and play at night, and it went well as far as that goes, but then I got a chance to do an actual record date, rehearsing for a week and then recording — a real professional recording session, not just a home taping or anything. And I wanted to do it and they wouldn’t let me off to do it so I quit. And my mom was a little alarmed.
You know Eddie Bert had a fantastic story.

I thought I’d be able to make it, I think I’m going to be okay. By that time I was 19, was already getting calls to play with a lot of people, was playing with really bass players like Red, and Gary Peacock was a friend and he really liked my playing ‘cause I was more adventurous than the people he played with. And he was, you know what happened to him?
